title: Measuring How We Reason: The New Blueprint for AI-Era Learning
author: Mike Kentz
summary: Kentz reviews the Stanford/ETS white paper 'Responsible Assessment in the AI Era,' produced from a January convening of 100 researchers, which declares single-event, product-based testing obsolete. Generative AI did not break traditional assessment—it merely exposed existing cracks, since grading only final products now risks measuring technological fluency rather than genuine human capability. The paper's alternative is process data: the record of actions, steps, and timing a learner takes while navigating a challenge. Conversational learning and interactive simulations emerge as uniquely powerful tools because they generate rich process data, naturally vary each run, and enable iterative feedback loops rather than one-time judgment events. Seven specific tools from the report—ranging from dialogue-based evidence systems to real-world conversational scenarios to interactive behavioral signals—illustrate how the field is operationalizing process-based evaluation at scale. Keeping humans in the loop remains essential so that AI scoring supports rather than replaces educator judgment.
points: Generative AI didn't break traditional assessment—it exposed a crack already there: grading only final products risks measuring technological fluency rather than authentic human capability.

Process data (the record of actions, steps, and timing a learner takes while working through a task) is the proposed alternative—shifting evaluation from inspecting finished products to observing how students think in real time.

Conversational simulations inherently support iteration: because each run varies naturally, students can receive targeted feedback on their reasoning, adjust strategy, and try again—turning evaluation from a one-time anxiety event into an ongoing learning loop.

The paper's seven example tools span dialogue-based evidence systems, AI role-play partners, behavioral signal readings from open-ended environments, and formal interaction rubrics—collectively expanding our definition of valid evidence.
Keeping humans in the loop (Section 4.3.c) remains a core principle: interactive evidence should empower educators rather than fully automate high-stakes decisions.
quotes: Generative AI did not break it; it simply exposed the crack that was already there.
grading only final products risks measuring a student's technological fluency rather than their actual human capability.
process data as the record of actions, steps, and timing a learner takes while working through a task

When a student works through an assignment by engaging in a live dialogue with an AI system, every prompt, reframe, and response generates a rich stream of process data. The resulting transcript becomes a map of their thinking rather than just a polished, potentially ghostwritten final draft.
Evaluation ceases to be a single, anxiety-inducing judgment event and becomes an ongoing learning loop.
When a hundred researchers convene at Stanford and agree that static, single-event testing is no longer serving us, it is a huge signal for where the field is heading.
